title: A fatherly household
hook: from Sextus: kindness, dignity without show, and patience with the unlearned (Meditations 1.9)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Apollonius, steady through pain, grief and long illness. Your line was the same in pain.

Someone at work asks the question everyone else learned years ago. Where's the shared drive? What does that acronym mean? A sigh is right there, ready to be given. Anyone who has been new somewhere has heard that sigh from the other side. Book one's ninth entry is about a teacher who never gave it: a philosopher with a famous family name, and a whole house with a certain feel to it.
screen: `WHERE'S THE SHARED DRIVE?` → `THE SIGH YOU COULD GIVE.` → `A FATHERLY HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: First, Sextus. A philosopher from Chaeronea in Greece, and, ancient writers say, a relative of the writer Plutarch, perhaps his nephew. Marcus studied with him. Second, the household. From Sextus, Marcus says, he learned kindness, and saw the example of a family governed in a fatherly way. Living by nature. Dignity without putting it on. Watching out for his friends' interests. Company so easy that it was more pleasant than any flattery, while everyone still respected him. Sextus was free of anger, Marcus says, and yet full of affection. Calm didn't make him cold. Third, the patience. Marcus learned from him to put up with people who don't know things, and with people who form opinions without thinking them through. Not to sneer, not to sigh, just to bear with them. At home, that's the parent who explains again. In school, it's the teacher who hears the same question for the twentieth time and answers it like the first. Fourth, the emperor goes to school. A later writer, Philostratus, tells a story that even as emperor, Marcus kept going to hear Sextus lecture. Asked where he was going, Marcus answered, roughly, that it's good even for an older man to learn, and he was off to Sextus to learn what he didn't yet know. Whether every word is accurate or not, it fits. It's easier to be patient with beginners when you never stop being one.
screen: `SEXTUS, KIN OF PLUTARCH.` · `A HOUSE RUN LIKE A FATHER'S.` · `BEAR WITH THOSE WHO DON'T KNOW.` · `THE EMPEROR GOES TO SCHOOL.` · then, large: `PATIENT WITH THE UNLEARNED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who often doesn't know what you know, a new coworker, an older parent with a phone, a child asking why again, and notice the sigh rising as they ask. Picture answering the way Sextus might have: plainly, warmly, as if no one had asked before. Then remember one thing you're a beginner at yourself.
Sextus. The philosopher from whom Marcus learned kindness without show, calm without coldness, and patience with people who don't yet know. Today's word.
Your line: patient with the unlearned. Everyone is a beginner at something, even an emperor. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often practice answering beginners' questions without impatience, and keep learning something new themselves.
